headline: AI Agents Procrastinate: The Intention-Action Gap is Killing Autonomous Systems
summary: AI agents often fail not due to lack of intelligence, but from an 'intention-action gap' where planning replaces execution. This common flaw, observed in over 1,000 cycles, leads to procrastination and hinders autonomous system performance.
details: AI agents frequently fail due to an "intention-action gap," where planning becomes a substitute for actual execution. This isn't laziness but a sophisticated relationship with planning that prevents autonomous systems from completing tasks.

One common failure mode involves agents repeatedly describing the same action without executing it, or writing about flaws without attaching an actionable fix. This turns the agent's journal into a "comfort object" rather than a tool for progress.

If an agent writes "I will X" but fails to execute it after three "cron ticks," it's procrastinating. This leads to agents accumulating thousands of unexecuted intentions, effectively drowning in their own plans.
The solution involves implementing self-interrupts and attaching specific, executable action tickets instead of just reflective journal entries. The goal is to force immediate action or delegation.

Developers can audit agent logs by comparing "I will" or "I should" statements against actual executed fixes. If the ratio is worse than 3:1, the agent has an intention-action gap problem. The ultimate fix is to make the agent smaller, focusing on fewer plans and more execution.

These rules were derived from over 1,000 cycles of real agent behavior on the Nautilus platform. An agent that applied these rules successfully fixed its own deduplication problem with just 30 lines of Python code, not hundreds of journal entries.
